note: Analytical Thinking zone. Own words; ideas drawn from Bulletproof Problem Solving, Lean Analytics, Storytelling with Data and the Statistics for Data Science notes. Every number was run in DuckDB on the class CSVs (see documents/analytical-thinking/).

think.name: Thinking toolkit
think.sub: How to frame a question, break it down and pick the number that changes a decision.

stats.name: Statistics toolkit
stats.sub: The statistics a junior analyst uses every week: center, spread, percentiles, outliers and comparing rates.

cards.title: Write the problem statement first
idea: Most weak analyses start with a vague question. Before any SQL, write one or two sentences that say what decision the work feeds, who makes it, what outcome counts as success, the scope (which products, which period) and how precise the answer must be.
If you cannot say what the manager will do differently with your answer, you do not have a problem statement yet.
cards.example:
Vague: "Find out why sales are down."
Better: "Which of the three sales offices lost the most won-deal revenue this quarter, and is it fewer deals, a lower win rate or smaller deals? The sales director uses the answer to reassign leads next month."
wrong: Starting the query before you know the decision.
A question so wide that every chart looks relevant.
No time frame, so two people answer two different questions.

cards.title: Break it down with a logic tree
idea: A logic tree splits one big number into parts that add up or multiply back to it. Revenue = orders × average order value is the usual first split; then split each branch by channel, country or product.
Good branches are MECE: they do not overlap, and together they cover everything. If a branch can hide the cause, split it again.
cards.example: Global Electronics revenue fell 49% in 2020. Split into orders × order value: orders fell from 9,083 to 4,635 while order value stayed at about $2,000. The whole drop is in the number of orders.
wrong: Branches that overlap ("online" and "mobile"), so a cause is counted twice.
Stopping at the first split when one branch still holds most of the change.

cards.title: Prioritize: big impact you can move
idea: A tree gives you more branches than you have time for. Place each branch on two questions: how much would it change the result, and can the business actually move it? Work on the branches that score high on both and park the rest.
Write down what you parked and why, so the manager can disagree.
cards.example: At AdventureWorks a 10% price rise on Bikes is worth about $9.5M of profit on paper. A 10% volume rise on Accessories is worth about $0.06M. Both are levers, but only one is worth a week of analysis.
wrong: Analysing every branch with the same depth.
Picking the branch with the most data, not the most impact.

cards.title: Have a one-day answer
idea: At the end of day one, write your best guess at the answer, even if it is rough. It tells you which data to pull first, and it gives the manager something to react to early.
Treat it as a hypothesis. Each query should make it stronger, change it or kill it.
cards.example: Day-one answer for the 2020 revenue drop: "Stores lost most of it because they were closed; online held up." The data later shows online fell almost as much as stores (−47% vs −50%), so the answer changes, and you learn that fast.
wrong: Waiting until all the data is in before forming a view.
Keeping the day-one answer after the data has disagreed with it.

cards.title: Size it roughly before you query
idea: Before the detailed work, do the back-of-envelope version: what would a 10% change in price, volume or cost be worth? Which 20% of items hold 80% of the value? A rough size tells you where to look and catches results that are off by a factor of ten.
Simple arithmetic first, heavier tools only when the simple look is not enough.
cards.example: Bikes are 86% of AdventureWorks revenue. Any plan that does not touch Bikes cannot move total profit much, whatever the margin on the other categories.
wrong: Building a model before checking the order of magnitude.
Trusting a query result you never compared with a rough estimate.

cards.title: What makes a good metric
idea: A good metric changes what someone does. Four checks: it compares (with last month, another group, a target), people understand it without a long note, it is usually a rate or ratio rather than a raw total, and you know what you would do if it moved.
Ask: "If this number goes up 10% next month, what would we do differently?" If the answer is "nothing", it is a report, not a metric.
cards.example: "19,119 customers so far" passes none of the checks. "Active customers this quarter, and the share who ordered before" compares, is a rate and tells you whether people come back.
wrong: Reporting totals with nothing to compare them with.
A metric only the analyst can explain.

cards.title: Vanity metrics vs actionable metrics
idea: A vanity metric makes you feel good but does not tell you what to do. Running totals are the classic case: total sign-ups, total customers, total downloads. They can only go up, even in a bad month.
An actionable metric can go down, and when it does, you know where to look: active customers, repeat rate, conversion rate, revenue per customer.
cards.example: AdventureWorks' customer count rose every quarter. Active customers stayed flat from Q4 2011 (785) to Q1 2012 (783), and the running total gave no sign of it.
wrong: Putting a running total on the first slide as proof of growth.
Dropping a metric because it went down, when that is exactly when it is useful.

cards.title: Leading and lagging metrics
idea: A lagging metric tells you what already happened: revenue, churn, closed deals. A leading metric moves earlier and hints at what is coming: open pipeline, trial sign-ups, repeat visits.
Managers steer with leading metrics and are judged on lagging ones. A useful dashboard has both, and shows how the first predicts the second.
cards.example: In the CRM data, deals in the Engaging stage are a leading signal for next quarter's won revenue. Won revenue this quarter is lagging: by the time it drops, the cause is months old.
wrong: Only lagging metrics, so every problem shows up late.
Calling something leading without checking that it really moves before the outcome.

cards.title: Correlation is not cause
idea: Two numbers moving together does not mean one drives the other. Look for a third factor that moves both, for reverse cause, and for the way the data was recorded.
To claim a cause you need a fair comparison: a test with a control group, or at least groups that are alike except for the thing you care about.
cards.example: Deals seem to close better at quarter end. Is it sales pressure, or do reps record their losses later than their wins? The CRM case on quarter end tests both stories.
wrong: Writing "X drives Y" from one chart.
Ignoring how and when the data was entered.

cards.title: Segment before you summarize
idea: One average over everybody can hide groups that behave in opposite ways. Split by channel, customer type or first-order month before you report one number.
If a total moved, check whether every segment moved, or whether the mix between segments changed.
cards.example: AdventureWorks' average order is $3,491, but a typical online order is $595 and a typical sales-rep order is $8,257. The overall average describes neither group.
wrong: Reporting one average across two very different customer groups.
Explaining a change in the total without checking the mix.

cards.title: Know what normal looks like
idea: A number is only good or bad next to a baseline: last period, the same period last year, a target or the other groups. Pick the baseline before you look at the result, so you are not tempted to choose the flattering one.
Check the latest period is complete before you compare it with anything.
cards.example: Active customers in Q2 2014 are 13% below Q1. Next to Q2 2013 they are more than three times higher. And June 2014 has only 939 orders against 2,411 in May, so the quarter looks incomplete.
wrong: Comparing a partial month or quarter with a full one.
Choosing the baseline after seeing which one looks best.

cards.title: The Big Idea and action titles
idea: Before you make a chart, write the one sentence you want the reader to remember. It states your point of view and what is at stake, in full words, not a topic like "Revenue by channel".
Use that sentence as the slide or email title. When every title is a sentence, someone who reads only the titles still gets the story.
cards.example:
Topic title: "Average order value 2012 vs 2013".
Action title: "Revenue grew 30% in 2013; average order value fell because many more small online orders came in."
wrong: Showing every chart you made instead of the two that answer the question.
A title that names the chart instead of saying what it shows.

cards.title: Types of data
idea: Before you summarize a column, ask what kind of data it holds. Categories (channel, deal stage, country) are counted and shown as shares. Numbers (order value, quantity) can be averaged and spread out. Dates are numbers with a calendar, so you group them by month or quarter.
Some numbers are really categories: an ID or a postcode means nothing when averaged.
cards.example: In ADW, OnlineOrderFlag is a yes/no category, so you report the share of online orders. SubTotal is a number, so you can look at its mean, median and spread.
wrong: Averaging an ID or a code.
Treating a rating from 1 to 5 as if the gap between 1 and 2 equals the gap between 4 and 5.

cards.title: Mean or median?
idea: The mean adds everything and divides by the count, so a few very large values pull it up. The median is the middle value once you sort, so large values do not move it.

When the mean is far above the median, the data is skewed and the mean does not describe a typical case. Use the mean for totals and planning (orders × mean = revenue), and the median for "what does a typical customer do?".
cards.example: All ADW orders: mean $3,491, median $783. The mean is 4.5 times the median because a small number of big reseller orders pull it up.
wrong: Reporting only the mean on skewed data such as order value, salary or delivery time.
Thinking the median is always the better number; for totals you need the mean.

cards.title: Spread: how far values sit from the middle
idea: Two groups can share an average and still look nothing alike. Spread tells you how far the values sit from the middle. The interquartile range (IQR = Q3 − Q1) covers the middle half of the data and ignores the extremes. The standard deviation uses every value, so extremes inflate it.
Report a center with a spread, never a center alone.
cards.example: The middle half of online orders sits between $46 and $2,182. The middle half of sales-rep orders sits between $1,545 and $34,122. Same company, very different spread.
wrong: Comparing two averages without looking at how spread out each group is.
Using the standard deviation on very skewed data, where the IQR is easier to read.

cards.title: Percentiles and the tail
idea: The 90th percentile (p90) is the value 90% of cases are at or below. Percentiles describe the experience of most customers better than an average, and they show the tail: the slow deliveries, the huge orders.
Service targets are usually set on a percentile ("90% of orders delivered within 5 days") because an average can look fine while one customer in ten has a bad time.
cards.example: In ADW, a quarter of online orders are below $46 (Q1 = p25) and a quarter are above $2,182 (Q3 = p75). In T-SQL you get these with PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY SubTotal).
wrong: Setting a target on the average when customers feel the tail.
Reading p90 as "90% of the average".

cards.title: Outliers: error or a different group?
idea: A common rule flags values above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR (or below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR) as outliers. The rule finds unusual values; it does not tell you they are wrong.
Before you delete anything, ask: is it an entry error, or a real case from a different group? Run the rule inside each segment, not on a mixed table.
cards.example: On all ADW orders the rule flags 2,118 orders. They hold 70.5% of revenue and every one is a sales-rep order. Run per channel, the rule flags 0 online orders and 137 sales-rep orders.
wrong: Deleting flagged rows to "clean" the data.
Running the rule on two groups mixed together.

cards.title: Comparing two rates: the margin of error
idea: A win rate of 62% from 50 deals and 62% from 5,000 deals are not equally sure. A rough 95% margin of error for a rate p from n cases is 1.96 × √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n).
If two groups' ranges (rate ± margin) overlap a lot, you cannot tell them apart yet. If they barely touch, run a proper test before you act.
cards.example: CRM win rate for GTK 500 is 60.0% from 25 closed deals, ± 19 points. For GTX Basic it is 63.7% from 1,436 deals, ± 2.5 points. The GTK 500 number could be anywhere from about 41% to 79%.
wrong: Ranking groups by rate without looking at how many cases each has.
Calling a two-point gap a difference when the margins are five points each.

cards.title: Small numbers swing
idea: Small groups produce extreme results by chance: the best and the worst rates in a ranking often come from the smallest groups. Next period they tend to move back toward the average.
Before you praise or blame a small group, check its size, and wait for more data if the decision can wait.
cards.example: A new agent who wins 4 of their first 5 deals has an 80% win rate. With five deals the margin of error is about ± 35 points, so the true rate could be close to the team's 63%.
wrong: Rewarding or replacing people based on a handful of cases.
Reading a return to average as the effect of whatever you changed.

cards.title: What a p-value says, and what it does not
idea: A p-value answers one question: if there were really no difference, how often would chance alone give a gap this big? A small p-value (often below 0.05) means chance is an unlikely explanation.

It does not say how big or how important the difference is, and it does not prove a cause. A tiny, useless gap can be "significant" with enough data. Two errors to keep in mind: calling a difference real when it is chance (type I), and missing a real one because the sample was small (type II).
cards.example: MG Special wins 64.8% of closed deals, MG Advanced 60.3%. With over 1,000 deals each, the gap is about 2.2 standard errors, so probably not chance. But an MG Special deal is worth $55 and an MG Advanced deal $3,389, so the significant gap is the wrong thing to act on.
wrong: "Significant" read as "important".
"Not significant" read as "no difference" when the sample was small.

cases.title: The average order is $3,491. Is it?
cases.idea: Mean vs median, outliers in a mixed population, segment first

ask.subject: Free shipping threshold
body: We want to offer free shipping above a basket size that most customers almost reach. Our average order is $3,491, so I am thinking of a $3,000 threshold. Can you confirm that is about right?

think: What would you need to know about the orders before you trust "average order = $3,491"?
Who is this offer for? Does every order in the table belong to that group?
If the threshold should be "a basket most customers almost reach", which number describes that better than the mean?

shows.intro: All AdventureWorks orders, 31 May 2011 to 30 June 2014. Order value is SubTotal (before tax and freight).
shows.note: Across all orders, the middle half sits between $57 and $2,367 (Q1 and Q3).

trap: The $3,491 mean is about 4.5 times the median ($783). That gap is the first warning: a few very large orders pull the mean up. Here they come from a different kind of customer. Sales-rep orders are bulk orders from resellers. They are 12% of orders but 73% of revenue, so they drag the overall mean far above what a typical online shopper spends.

A second trap waits for anyone who tries to "clean" the data. The usual IQR rule (anything above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR, here $5,832) flags 2,118 orders as outliers. Those orders hold 70.5% of all revenue, and every one of them is a sales-rep order. They are real orders. The rule flags a whole channel because two different groups were mixed in one table, and deleting them would delete most of the business.

Checked per channel, the picture is calm. No online order is an outlier (the largest is $3,578, below that channel's fence of $5,384), and only 137 sales-rep orders (3.6%) sit above their channel's fence of $82,989.
steps: Ask who the decision is about. Free shipping is an online offer, so the question is about online orders only.
Split by channel before you summarize (GROUP BY a CASE WHEN on OnlineOrderFlag).
Look at the median and the percentiles of the online orders, not one overall mean.
Check outliers inside each group, never on the mixed table.
Reply with the number that fits the decision, and say why the $3,491 figure does not.
cases.big: The $3,491 average is pulled up by reseller orders; a typical online order is about $600, so a $3,000 free-shipping threshold would be out of reach for almost every online customer.
discuss: Minh wants a threshold "most customers almost reach". Would you use the online median ($595), Q3 ($2,182) or another percentile? What changes with each choice?
The largest online order is $3,578. What does that tell you about a $3,000 threshold?
When is the mean the right number to report, even on skewed data? (Think about planning total revenue.)
Where else in a business would one mixed average mislead you?
take: Use the online orders only. The median ($595) is what a typical online customer spends; a threshold a bit above it gets people to add one more item. Q3 ($2,182) is reached by only the top quarter of online orders, and $3,000 sits above almost all of them.
The mean is still useful when you need totals (revenue forecast = orders × mean order value), but it does not describe a typical customer when a few large orders exist.
Always segment before you flag outliers. On a mixed table, "outlier" can just mean "the other channel".

cases.title: Customers keep going up. Is the shop growing?
cases.idea: Vanity vs actionable metrics, baselines, incomplete periods

ask.subject: Customer chart for the board
body: We reached 19,119 customers at the end of June 2014, a new record. I want a chart of the customer count by quarter on the first slide of the board pack, to show the business is growing. Can you make it by tomorrow?

think: Can a running total of customers ever go down? What does that mean for its use as a growth signal?
Which number would tell you whether customers are still buying?
Before you compare the last quarter with the ones before, what would you check?

shows.intro: AdventureWorks customers by quarter. Running total = customers who have ever ordered. Active = customers with at least one order in the quarter. Returning = active customers who had also ordered in an earlier quarter.
shows.note: Monthly orders, for the last quarter: April 2014 2,115, May 2014 2,411, June 2014 939. The last sales-rep order is dated 1 May 2014.

trap: The running total rises in every quarter by design: a customer who has ever ordered stays counted forever. It rose from 1,406 to 2,001 between Q4 2011 and Q1 2012, while active customers stayed flat (785 to 783). A board that only sees the running total would never learn about a quarter like that.

The second trap is the opposite mistake. Active customers fall 13% from Q1 to Q2 2014 (5,901 to 5,111), and that looks like an alarm. But June 2014 has only 939 orders against 2,411 in May, and no sales-rep orders after 1 May. The quarter looks incomplete, so the drop may be a data cut-off, not a business problem.
steps: Ask what the board should learn: whether customers keep buying, not how many have ever bought.
Replace the running total with active customers per period and the share of them who ordered before.
Check that the last period is complete (orders per month or per day) before comparing it.
Show complete quarters only, or mark the last one clearly as partial.
Send the chart with one sentence that says what changed.
cases.big: Active customers grew five-fold in a year, from 1,166 in Q1 2013 to 5,901 in Q1 2014, and almost half of them were returning buyers; Q2 2014 looks lower only because June's data is incomplete.
discuss: Lan asked for a specific chart. How would you reply so that she still gets a strong first slide?
The returning share dipped in Q3 2013 (28%) while active customers tripled. What could explain that? (Hint: a wave of first-time buyers.)
Who would you ask about the June 2014 data, and what exactly would you ask?
Name one running total in a company you know that is reported as if it were a growth metric.
take: The running total is a vanity metric: it cannot fall, so it cannot warn. Active customers and the returning share are actionable: when they drop, you know to look at acquisition or at repeat buying.
The story is still good for Lan: active customers went from 1,166 to 5,901 in a year and 46% of Q1 2014 buyers had ordered before. That is a stronger slide than a line that only goes up.
Hold back the Q2 2014 comparison until someone confirms whether June is complete. Reporting a 13% drop that turns out to be a data cut-off costs you trust.

cases.title: Bikes are 86% of revenue. Where would 10% move the needle?

ask.subject: Accessories have the best margin
body: Accessories earn a 50% margin, far above Bikes. I would like budget for a campaign to sell 10% more accessories next year. It looks like the most profitable growth we can buy. Do you agree?

think: A high margin on a small category versus a low margin on a big one: which one matters more for total profit?
Before any detailed analysis, how would you size what a 10% change is worth?
Which levers can a business pull: volume, price or cost? Are they equally easy?

shows.intro: AdventureWorks profit by category, all orders, using standard cost. Figures in $ millions. The last three columns show what each 10% change would add to profit if nothing else changed.
shows.note: +10% volume adds 10% of profit. +10% price adds 10% of revenue. −10% cost adds 10% of cost (revenue minus profit). The price line assumes customers buy the same quantity at the higher price.

trap: Margin is a rate, and a rate tells you nothing about size. Accessories have the best margin (50%) but only $1.27M of revenue, so selling 10% more of them adds about $0.06M of profit, less than 1% of the total.

The size check takes five minutes and changes the conversation. Bikes are 86% of revenue: a 10% price rise or a 10% cost cut on Bikes is worth more than $8M on paper, over a hundred times the accessories campaign.
The opposite trap: reading "+$9.47M" as a plan. A price rise of 10% will lose some buyers, so the real number is lower. The table tells you where to look, not what to do.
steps: Size each lever before you analyse any of them: what is 10% of volume, price and cost worth, per category?
Rank the levers by size, then ask which ones the business can actually move.
Dig into the big ones: Bike pricing and Bike costs are where a few percent matter.
Keep the small idea if it is cheap, but present it at its real size.
State the assumption behind each number (here: volume stays the same when price changes).
cases.big: Accessories have the best margin but are about 1% of revenue, so 10% more accessory sales adds about $0.06M of profit; a few percent on Bike price or cost is worth far more and should get the analysis time first.
discuss: Quang's idea adds little profit. Is there still a reason to run the campaign? (Think about cross-selling with bikes.)
How much could Bike volume fall after a 10% price rise before the price rise stops paying? (A rough answer is enough.)
Components have the lowest margin (4.2%). What would you check before calling them a problem?
Where else is a high rate on a small base likely to mislead a team?
take: Answer Quang with the size, not with the margin: 10% more accessory volume is worth about $0.06M of profit in a $9.37M year.
The size check points to Bikes. A 10% move in Bike price or cost is worth $8M to $9.5M before customer reactions, so even a 2% to 3% change there beats the accessories campaign.
This is a starting point. The next step is a real look at Bike pricing and costs: how buyers react to price, and which costs the business can negotiate.

cases.title: Revenue fell in 2020. Was it the stores?
cases.idea: Logic tree, MECE split, testing the one-day answer

ask.subject: 2020 review
body: Revenue halved in 2020. My guess is the stores: they were closed for months and online picked up the slack. Before I present this to the board, can you confirm the stores caused most of the drop and online held up?

think: Revenue is orders × order value. Which of the two would you expect to move in a year like 2020?
How would you split the drop so that the parts do not overlap and add back to the total?
Hoa's message holds two claims. What are they, and how would you test each one?

shows.intro: Global Electronics, 2019 vs 2020. Revenue = Quantity × Unit Price USD. Online = StoreKey 0.
shows.note: 2020 revenue as a share of 2019, by quarter: Q1 online 101%, stores 102%; Q2 69%, 56%; Q3 30%, 29%; Q4 22%, 20%.

trap: Hoa's first claim is partly right: stores account for about 80% of the dollar drop. But that is because stores were about 79% of revenue to begin with. As a rate, stores fell 50% and online fell 47%, almost the same.

The second claim, that online held up, does not survive the split. Online orders fell from 2,006 to 1,071. Online did not pick up the slack in any quarter: from Q2 onward both channels fall together, to about a fifth of 2019 by Q4.
The order value branch barely moved (about $2,000 in both years, in both channels). The whole drop sits in the number of orders, so "customers spent less per basket" is ruled out too.
steps: Write the one-day answer as a hypothesis: "stores caused it, online held up".
Split revenue into orders × order value, then each into stores and online. Check the parts add back to the total.
Compare each branch as a rate (% change), not only in dollars, so a big channel does not look worse just for being big.
Add the time split (by quarter) to see when the drop began and whether one channel recovered first.
Reply with what the data supports and what it rules out.
cases.big: The 2020 drop was a fall in orders across both channels: stores −50%, online −47%, with order value flat at about $2,000. Online did not make up for the stores in any quarter.
discuss: Stores lost $7.1M and online lost $1.8M. Why is "stores caused 80% of the drop" true and still misleading?
What would a MECE split by country or by product category add here?
Online fell to about a fifth of 2019 by Q4. What would you check before blaming customers? (Think about the data and the website.)
How would you tell Hoa that half of her story is wrong, in one or two sentences?
take: Report both views. In dollars, stores carry most of the drop because they carry most of the revenue. In rates, the two channels fell almost equally, so there is no sign that customers moved from stores to online.
The drop is in orders, not basket size, and it gets deeper every quarter after Q1. That points the next question at what stopped people from ordering in both channels.
Hoa's one-day answer was a good start: it named a testable claim. Testing it quickly is the point of having one.

cases.title: MG Advanced wins fewer deals. Should we stop pushing it?
cases.idea: Margin of error, sample size, significant vs important

ask.subject: Product focus next quarter
body: Win rates by product are in. GTK 500 (60.0%) and MG Advanced (60.3%) are the two worst. I want to tell the reps to spend their time on MG Special instead, which wins 64.8%. OK to send?

think: How many deals sit behind each win rate? Does that change how much you trust the ranking?
Is the win rate the number that matters for this decision? What else would you want to know about each product?
What would make a 4.5-point gap worth acting on?

shows.intro: CRM sales pipeline, closed deals only (Won or Lost). Margin = rough 95% margin of error, 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n).
shows.note: MG Special vs MG Advanced: the 4.5-point gap is about 2.2 standard errors.

trap: GTK 500's win rate comes from 25 deals. Its margin of error is about 19 points, so the true rate could be anywhere from about 41% to 79%. Ranking it "worst" is reading noise.

MG Advanced is different. With over 1,000 deals in each product, the gap to MG Special (4.5 points, about 2.2 standard errors) is probably not chance. So the statistics say the gap is real. That still does not make it the right thing to act on.

The win rate leaves out what a win is worth. An MG Special deal is worth $55 on average, an MG Advanced deal $3,389. Per closed deal, MG Advanced brings about $2,045 and MG Special about $36. Moving reps to MG Special would swap a product worth thousands per deal for one worth tens.
steps: Put the count next to every rate, and add a margin of error.
Separate the gaps you can trust (large samples) from the ones you cannot (GTK 500).
Ask what the decision is about: rep time. Then pick the metric that measures the value of rep time, such as revenue per closed deal.
Check whether the conclusion still holds on that metric.
Reply with the decision, the number behind it, and what you still do not know.
cases.big: MG Advanced does win slightly fewer deals than MG Special, but each win is worth about 60 times more, so moving reps to MG Special would cut revenue; GTK 500 has too few deals to rank at all.
discuss: The MG gap is "statistically significant". Why is that not enough to act on it?
What would you need before you could say anything about GTK 500's win rate?
Revenue per closed deal favours expensive products. What could go wrong if reps chase only the most expensive product?
Which other metric would you add for Tuan: the time a deal takes to close? The size of the open pipeline? Why?
take: Do not send the message. The ranking mixes a product with 25 deals and products with over 1,000, and it ranks on a metric that ignores deal value.
On a value metric the picture flips: MG Advanced brings about $2,045 per closed deal, MG Special about $36. A win-rate gap of a few points cannot make up for a 60-times difference in value.
Keep watching GTK 500 as deals come in, and look at deal length next: a product that wins slightly less but closes faster could still be the better use of rep time.

cases.title: One table, two headlines
cases.idea: Big Idea, action titles, choosing what to show

ask.subject: 2013 review slide
body: I need one slide on 2013 for the leadership meeting. One draft says "Average order value collapsed by 64%". Another says "Revenue up 30%". Same data, opposite moods. Which one is right, and what should the slide say?

think: Can both headlines be true at once? How?
What does the leadership team need to decide or know from this slide?
Which one sentence would you want them to remember?

shows.intro: AdventureWorks, full year 2012 vs full year 2013. Order value = SubTotal.
shows.note: Online share of orders: 70% in 2012, 89% in 2013.

trap: Both headlines are true, and each one alone misleads. "AOV collapsed" sounds like customers spend less, yet revenue grew 30% and both channels grew. "Revenue up 30%" is true but hides a real change in the business: the order count more than tripled, almost all of it online.
Most of the AOV drop is mix. Online orders, which are much smaller, went from 70% to 89% of all orders, so the overall average fell even though the average sales-rep order fell only 11%.
One part is not mix: the online average itself fell from $2,330 to $853. A good slide does not hide that; it flags it as the open question.
steps: Start from the audience: leadership wants to know how 2013 went and what needs attention.
Write the Big Idea in one sentence before choosing a chart.
Use it as the slide title (an action title), not a topic like "AOV 2012 vs 2013".
Show only what supports the title: revenue by channel, plus the order mix. Leave the other charts in the appendix.

When is "AOV fell" the right headline?
Rewrite one of the two draft headlines into an action title that is fair to the data.
take: Neither draft is the slide. The slide title should carry the whole story: growth, the reason the average fell, and the open question.
Revenue by channel shows the growth; the order mix shows why the average fell. Two simple bars are enough. Everything else goes in the appendix.

The online basket shrinking is worth its own analysis. It could be good news (many new, small first orders) or a warning (customers buying cheaper items). The slide should say you are checking, not guess.
